newsitem.title: FRANCE: FEATURE - French women look to Joan of Arc for inspiration.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - French women look to Joan of Arc for inspiration.

text.p: In the nation that created the word chauvinism, French women are drawing inspiration from the example of 15th century warrior Joan of Arc in efforts to bolster their featherweight political clout.

Women in France have the most dismal parliamentary record in the European Union, behind Greece and Britain, with just 5.5 percent of the seats in the National Assembly. And the heads of the biggest 200 French firms are, without exception, men.

By contrast with a lack of power overall, some French women have become icons -- from Nobel prize winning scientist Marie Curie, who discovered radium, to Brigitte Bardot, who switched from actress and sex symbol to animal rights campaigner.
In a new drive to make French politics less male dominated, the opposition Socialist Party is promising that 30 percent of its candidates in 1988 legislative elections will be female.

And 10 women politicians, including France's first and only woman prime minister Socialist Edith Cresson, who ruled for a scant 10 months in 1991-92, are urging a constitutional amendment to impose quotas to feminise politics.
"We can no longer allow France to stay at the bottom of the European class and let a macho, retrograde caste continue to confiscate power," said ex-Socialist culture minister Jack Lang.

Allies of conservative Prime Minister Alain Juppe have denounced the Socialist quota plan as a gimmick. They oppose a constitutional amendment, saying equality was enshrined by the 1789 French Revolution that abolished the monarchy.
"Equality exists in French law," said junior employment minister Anne-Marie Couderc. But she said women now had a chance because all parties agreed something had to be done.
It may be a long haul.
Janine Mossuz-Lavau, a sociologist and co-author of a book due out in January about French women, said the Revolution was more chauvinistic than France likes to recall.
"It gave rights to everyone except women," she said, saying male revolutionaries feared women were too pro-clerical and monarchist.

Napoleon aggravated discrimination in a civil code that meant women needed their husbands' permission even to get a passport until 1938. Nicolas Chauvin was one of Napoleon's most loyal followers, spawning the word "chauvinism" to describe aggressive nationalism or supposed male superiority.
France dragged its feet for decades before General Charles de Gaulle granted women the vote in 1944 in recognition of their role in the wartime Resistance movement.
Until then, the move was blocked for fear that church-going women would elect conservative governments that would roll back landmark secularist laws passed in the early 20th century.
In the National Assembly, women now have 32 seats out of 577, or 5.5 percent.

Women's tiny share of power is paradoxical in France, where 60 percent work, roughly the EU average. And French women have overthrown Roman Catholic resistance to win liberal laws on issues ranging from child benefits to birth control.
Women are well represented, for instance, as teachers, doctors, magistrates or journalists.

Even though women have scant influence in parliament, opinion polls show that Simone Veil, a former centrist health minister and survivor of a Nazi death camp, and former Socialist labour minister Martine Aubry are among the most respected politicians in France.
Although France's women's liberation movement has faltered, Frenchwomen were once international pioneers. Author Simone de Beauvoir's 1949 work "The Second Sex" became a textbook for feminism.
Women perhaps fare worst in France's boardrooms.
"The business world is even more misogynist than politics," said Jean-Michel Quatrepoints, editor of the Top Management Guide which shows no women head any of the largest 200 firms.
Juppe has disappointed women since President Jacques Chirac came to power in May 1995 promising "more feminine" government.
Juppe named 12 women to his first cabinet, which he trumpeted as a record 30 percent. But he sacked eight of them in a reshuffle last year, cutting their share to an unexceptional 13 percent.

Socialist Cresson, who left office in 1992 with polls showing she was the least popular premier in modern history, was one of the first women to wield power since Joan of Arc led armies against the English in the 15th century.
Burnt at the stake as a witch in 1431 after being betrayed to the English, Joan was canonized in 1921.
Apart from Joan of Arc, most of the women in French history books are royal mistresses such as Madame de Pompadour who influenced the weak-willed King Louis XV in the 18th century.

And Marie-Antoinette, beheaded with her husband Louis XVI during the Revolution, came up with one of history's most infamous one-liners, reputedly exclaiming "Let them eat cake" when told the poor were starving for lack of bread.
Among the best known women in modern France are past and present screen goddesses like Bardot, Catherine Deneuve or Isabelle Adjani and television interviewer Anne Sinclair.
Chirac has set up a special "Equality Watch" commission to examine how to give women more clout.

Sweden, with a parliament where 40.4 percent of deputies are women, leads Norway, Finland and Denmark at the top of a ranking of more than 100 countries compiled by the Geneva-based Inter-Parliamentary Union on the representation of women.
France has slipped below Greece, where women hold 6.3 percent of parliamentary seats after elections in September, at the bottom of the EU ranking.
Asked once about the prospect that France would elect a female president, Cresson replied: "Not for 100 years".
